analysis.one_liner: Strengthens penalties and enforcement for women paid less than men for the same work.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 247-178 with 233 of 235 Democrats in favor, but it never got a vote in the Senate and died when that Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strengthen the Equal Pay Act, the 1963 law banning pay discrimination between men and women doing the same work. It would let workers recover compensatory and punitive damages from employers who underpay them because of their sex, let them join class-action suits without signing on individually, and protect them from being punished for discussing their wages. It would also narrow the excuses employers can offer for a pay gap, require federal collection of pay data by sex and race, and fund salary-negotiation training for women.
analysis.who_benefits: Women who are paid less than male colleagues for the same or similar work, and workers generally who could face retaliation for sharing wage information. The bill's findings state that pay gaps depress wages for working families and undermine women's retirement security.

how_it_helps.text: Adds compensatory damages, and punitive damages where the employer acted with malice or reckless indifference, on top of the back-pay awards already available under the Equal Pay Act.

Allows Equal Pay Act cases to proceed as class actions, with individuals joined as plaintiffs without their written consent, and shifts the burden to the employer to prove that a pay gap rests on a bona fide factor like education, training, or experience that is job-related and consistent with business necessity.
Bars employers from retaliating against employees who inquire about, discuss, or disclose their own or a coworker's wages.
Directs the EEOC to issue regulations collecting pay information from employers by the sex, race, and national origin of employees for use in enforcing pay-discrimination laws.
Authorizes a grant program for salary-negotiation skills training for girls and women and a $15 million appropriation for training, research, and small-business compliance assistance.

analysis.who_pays: Employers found to have discriminated on pay would owe larger awards and face class-wide suits, and all covered employers would take on new reporting duties and litigation risk; those costs would ultimately come out of business earnings, prices, or hiring decisions. Small businesses exempt from the Fair Labor Standards Act would be exempt from the bill.

drawbacks.text: Businesses argued the bill would multiply lawsuits: it eases class actions, adds punitive damages, and replaces the old broad employer defense with a business-necessity test that a worker can defeat by showing a cheaper alternative practice the employer refused to adopt, so legitimate pay differences based on merit or market rates could draw legal challenges.

The bill treats employees working for the same employer anywhere in the same county as comparable for pay-comparison purposes, which extends coverage beyond workers at the same worksite and was a contested change.

A House Republican motion to recommit, which would have sent the bill back to committee with an amendment, drew 189 votes including 188 Republicans, showing that more than half the House's minority viewed the enforcement changes as overbroad even while the bill passed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the benefit is concrete: pay discrimination today is hard to prove, penalties are limited to back pay, and pay secrecy makes gaps hard to discover, and the bill attacks all three. For employers, the cost is real but targeted: it falls on those with unexplained sex-based pay gaps, and the strongest objection, that it invites a wave of litigation, is partly answered by the bill's own limits, such as the small-business exemption, the malice-or-recklessness threshold for punitive damages, and the requirement that employer defenses be genuinely job-related. The main fair criticism is the county-wide comparison rule, which reaches farther than the same-job-site standard it replaced.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on a mostly party-line vote of 247-178, but the Senate referred it to its health, education, and labor committee, which never brought it to a vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced by Rep. Rosa DeLauro with 230 cosponsors, 229 of them Democrats.
The House Education and Labor Committee reported the bill amended by a vote of 26-17 on July 28, 2008.
A Republican motion to recommit failed 189-236, with all but one Democrat voting no and all but four Republicans voting yes.
The House passed the bill 247-178 on July 31, 2008: every voting Democrat in favor, and 14 of 199 Republicans in favor.

The Senate received the bill on August 1, 2008 and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, where no further action was taken before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who could have faced expanded damages, class actions, and pay-data reporting under the bill, since none of it took effect. Women seeking stronger equal-pay enforcement had to wait for a later Congress.

for.name: Rep. Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it through the House.

for.name: Rep. George Miller
for.role: Chair, House Education and Labor Committee
for.what_they_did: Brought the bill through markup and reported it amended by a 26-17 committee vote.

against.name: 178 of 199 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage and nearly all voted for the motion to recommit to add an amendment.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on August 1, 2008 and took no action; no hearing, markup, or vote followed before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: House Democrats were unanimous in support (233-0) while Republicans were 178-14 against, and the Senate, where Democrats held a narrow majority, never acted.

industries.note: The bill would expose employers with unexplained sex-based pay gaps to compensatory and punitive damages, class actions without written employee consent, and a narrowed business-necessity defense, plus new EEOC pay-data reporting. The cost lands on businesses whose pay practices cannot be justified as job-related.

Class-action enforcement and pay transparency strengthen workers' ability to challenge wage gaps, which unions have long pursued; unionized employers are also subject to the same enforcement machinery.
